analysis.one_liner: Creates a Justice Department system where journalists can file complaints about law enforcement misconduct.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote after being introduced in October 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Attorney General to build an online system where members of the press — defined broadly to include anyone gathering news for the public — could file complaints, anonymously if they choose, about misconduct by federal, state, or local police. Agencies would be notified within 30 days and would have to respond with details of the incident within 60 days, including any recordings and any property searched or seized. A state or local government that failed to respond would lose half of its Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funding the following year, and states that ignored three or more complaints in a year would be cut off from the Pentagon's 1033 program of surplus military equipment. The Justice Department would also have to publish an annual public report of all complaints, with names redacted.
analysis.who_benefits: Journalists and news organizations covering protests and police activity would gain a documented, trackable way to report mistreatment — including beatings, seizures of cameras, or destruction of press materials — directly to the Justice Department. The public would gain an annual, publicly available record of complaints against police agencies, and taxpayers would benefit because federal grant money would flow away from agencies that refuse to explain their conduct.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Attorney General to create an electronic complaint system open to members of the press, allowing anonymous filings and photo, video, and audio attachments [S3].

Law enforcement agencies named in a complaint must respond within 60 days with the date, officers involved, a detailed description of the incident, the legal justification offered, any property searched, damaged, or seized, and any recordings [S3].
A state or local government that fails to comply faces a 50 percent cut to its Byrne Justice Assistance Grant the following year, with the withheld money shifted to compliant states [S3].

States that fail to respond to three or more complaints in a fiscal year lose access to the Defense Department's 1033 program of surplus military equipment until the Defense Secretary and Attorney General determine they are back in compliance [S3].
The Attorney General must publish a year-end public report compiling the complaints, with personally identifiable information redacted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Police departments and other law enforcement agencies would bear the cost: they would face a 60-day response deadline for each complaint, the possibility of losing half their federal justice grants, and potential exclusion from free surplus military equipment. The Justice Department would fund and administer the new complaint system and annual report.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and the DOJ

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'member of the press' as essentially anyone gathering news through mass media, a deliberately broad definition that critics could argue is hard to administer and could draw filings from nearly anyone claiming a news purpose [S3].

The complaint responses are due to the Justice Department but the bill does not require the underlying complaints or responses to be individually published — only a redacted year-end compilation — so the accountability value depends on the department of the day actually using it [S3].

The funding penalty is blunt: a 50 percent cut to Byrne grants punishes an entire state or city government, including its innocent residents and officers, for an agency's failure to answer a complaint within 60 days [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is simple and narrow — a complaint intake system plus a funding stick — rather than new criminal or civil liability for police, which lowers the risk of overreach. The main honest costs are the grant-cut penalty falling on whole governments rather than individual wrongdoers, and the fact that outcomes depend on the Justice Department's willingness to act on what it receives. On balance the accountability gain for press freedom and public transparency outweighs the administrative and funding risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on October 1, 2020, and sat there until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on October 1, 2020 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and that was the final action recorded for the bill [S5].
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill established a Justice Department press complaint system with funding penalties for law enforcement agencies that failed to respond within 60 days [S2].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without the House ever taking the bill up [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off: they face no new complaint-response obligation, no risk of losing Byrne grant funds, and no threat to their access to 1033 military equipment. Journalists and the public do not get the complaint and reporting system.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought to create the DOJ press complaint system with grant and 1033 program penalties.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 1, 2020 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors and received no Republican support in the record, and the Republican-chaired-era House leadership agenda never advanced it; no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local police)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to answer press misconduct complaints within 60 days on pain of losing half their Byrne grant funds and access to 1033 military equipment. Agencies that avoid transparency pay nothing today; the bill's failure preserves that status quo.

industries.industry: Defense Department surplus equipment (1033 program) participants
industries.note: States ignoring repeated press complaints would have been cut off from free military surplus equipment. The bill's failure leaves the 1033 program's terms unchanged.
Reporters covering protests and police activity would have gained an official complaint channel with a paper trail and a public annual report. The channel never opened.
